appraisal_events.evidence: Swann hopes Odette will die painlessly in an accident and feels himself close to Mahomet II, who stabbed a beloved wife 'afin de retrouver sa liberté d'esprit'; he then indicts his own selfishness ('il faisait si bon marché de la vie d'Odette'), and later, in pursuing 'sincerity' from her, the narrator states flatly that he lied as much as Odette did and 'n'était pas moins égoïste,' ending the passage sitting apart from her, afraid to embrace her, watching their love die.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator repeatedly exposes Swann's jealousy as morally corrosive and self-serving across the passage, from his murderous fantasy and self-comparison to a wife-killing sultan through his manipulative feigned love of truth, culminating in an estranged, fearful posture toward Odette.

appraisal_events.evidence: Odette confirms Swann's suspicion that her claimed solo trip is really a trip with Forcheville ('Oui mon petit, nous partons le 19...'), and Swann can no longer separate this from his belated memory of Mme Verdurin's teasing intimacy with her ('tu n'es pas de marbre') and open affection ('elle m'embrasse... elle veut que je la tutoie').
appraisal_events.explanation: Odette's local credibility is undermined by a confirmed lie about traveling with Forcheville and by a retrospectively suspicious memory implicating Mme Verdurin, though the narrator explicitly calls the anonymous letter's more lurid accusations against her implausible, so this discredit remains partly Swann's own jealous construction.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is left emotionally degraded by jealousy: reduced to wishing Odette dead, manipulating her under the guise of loving sincerity, and finally too estranged to embrace her.
The narrator directly judges Swann as no less egoistic and dishonest than Odette in his pursuit of the truth, lowering him morally within the passage.

Odette's standing is somewhat lowered by her confirmed deception about the Forcheville trip and by unresolved suspicion tied to Mme Verdurin, tempered by the narrator's explicit skepticism toward the anonymous letter's other accusations.

ambiguities: The extended middle section, where Swann in turn suspects M. de Charlus, the prince des Laumes, M. d'Orsan, Rémi, the narrator's grandfather, Bergotte, le peintre, and the Verdurins of writing the anonymous letter, resolves into no stable verdict (he ends up shaking all their hands as before), so it is read as evidence of Swann's own diminished, paranoid state (E1) rather than as independent evaluative events against those figures.

The negative movement toward Odette in E2 mixes a textually confirmed lie (the Egypt trip) with material the narrator explicitly frames as implausible (the anonymous letter's promiscuity claims) and with Swann's own speculative recollection of Mme Verdurin's affection toward her; no liaison is confirmed by the narrative, so the status effect for Odette is kept modest and the event's stance is marked uncertain.
